title: Samudera Pasai Sultanate
capsule: The Samudera Pasai Sultanate, located on the northeastern coast of Sumatra near modern Lhokseumawe, is considered the first Islamic sultanate in Southeast Asia; its founder Merah Silu converted to Sunni Islam and took the name Malik ul-Salih, with the sultanate typically dated to around 1267. Ibn Battuta visited in 1345 and described Sultan Ahmad Malik al-Zahir as a devout Shafi'i ruler presiding over a prosperous pepper and camphor trade; the court used gold dirham coinage and Old Malay as its administrative language. Samudera Pasai was eclipsed commercially by Malacca in the early 15th century, occupied by the Portuguese in 1521, and finally absorbed by the Aceh Sultanate under Sultan Ali Mughayat Syah in 1524.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. The core capital location is securely identified archaeologically at Beuringin (near Lhokseumawe), but the inland territorial extent of the sultanate's control is poorly documented and reconstructed largely from trade records and traveler accounts.
